links.note: Metallurgy glossed as the techniques of extracting metals from nature, purifying or combining them, and the scientific study of metals - that gloss sits in this concept. Already linked and correct.
Civilisation beginning in Mesopotamia about 6,000 years ago - this concept is the only one that dates and places the earliest civilisations.
The civilisation beginning around 2600 BCE - this concept dates the transition of towns into cities to that year. Already linked and correct.
Harappa as the first city of this civilisation to be excavated - the DON'T MISS OUT box in this concept, which explains the commonest name of the civilisation.
The First Urbanisation of India - this concept applies that phrase to the growth of towns into cities around 2600 BCE.
A tributary glossed as a river that flows into a larger river or lake, with the Yamuna into the Ganga as the example, appears in this concept's opening geography.
The Sarasvati known today as the Ghaggar in India and the Hakra in Pakistan - this concept is the one that gives the modern names and says the river is now seasonal.
The Sarasvati first mentioned and worshipped in the Rig Veda, both as a goddess and as a river flowing from mountain to sea - this concept's sentence.
A fortification glossed as a massive wall surrounding a settlement, generally for protective purposes - the gloss appears in this concept's description of the planned cities.
The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro, a small but elaborate tank measuring about 12 by 7 metres - this concept carries those dimensions.
A reservoir glossed as a large natural or artificial place where water is stored - the gloss sits in this concept beside Dholavira's reservoirs.
Barley among the cereals grown by the Harappans - this concept lists barley, wheat, some millets and sometimes rice.
The Harappans as the first in Eurasia to grow cotton, which they wove into clothes - this concept's claim, word for word.
The plough as a Harappan farming tool, some of which are still used by modern farmers - this concept is where the farming tools are described.
Carnelian as the reddish semiprecious stone found mostly in Gujarat and used for the most favoured beads - this concept's sentence.
Tin added to copper giving bronze, which is harder than copper - the DON'T MISS OUT box in this concept.
Lothal in Gujarat and its huge basin, 214 by 36 metres, inferred to be a dockyard - this concept's subject, not the Lothal pot concept.
Small objects bearing animal figures with writing signs above them are the seals this concept describes, excavated in thousands from many settlements.
Seals generally made of steatite, a soft stone hardened through heating - this concept's own detail.

The Dancing Girl figurine from Mohenjo-daro is discussed only in this concept, where the LET'S EXPLORE asks about her attitude and her bangles. The stem is truncated and opens mid-sentence at 8 cm high.
Naming one of the two factors currently agreed upon for the decline - this concept states both, the climatic change from 2200 BCE onward and the drying up of the Sarasvati in its central basin.
Listing three essential characteristics of a civilisation is answered straight from this concept's seven, and the model answer names government, urbanism and writing from that list.

Why productive agriculture is fundamental - this concept states it as enough to feed not just the villages but also the cities, and its THINK ABOUT IT asks which characteristic is essential to the development of all the others.

The geographical extent over the plains of the Indus and its tributaries and along the Sarasvati, across modern India and Pakistan - this concept's opening geography of Punjab, Sindh and the Sarasvati's course.

Why the term Indus Valley Civilisation is obsolete - this concept's THINK ABOUT IT says the word Valley is obsolete because the civilisation extended much beyond the Indus region, into the Sarasvati basin. Already linked and correct.

Evidence that the Harappans attended to water management and cleanliness - this concept opens on exactly that and supplies the bathing areas connected to a larger network of drains running below the streets.
How we know the Harappan diet - the animal and fish bones found in excavations and the scientific examination of clay pots revealing dairy, turmeric, ginger and banana are all in this concept.
The export list - ornaments, timber, objects of daily use, probably gold and cotton - is stated in this concept, with carnelian beads as the most favoured ornament.
The likely purpose of the seals, letting traders identify their goods and each other - this concept's opening inference, and its closing statement that the seals somehow relate to trade.
Harappan farming tools including the plough and what they were made of - this concept is the one that names the farming tools and notes some are still used today.
Evidence for maritime trade - this concept supplies both halves of the answer, quite a few settlements in the coastal regions of Gujarat and Sindh and Lothal's basin inferred to be a dockyard.
Why the Harappan script is undecipherable - this concept states that the writing system on the seals and the symbolic meaning of the animal figures are yet to be understood.

Naming objects of daily use found at Harappan sites - this concept is the two pages of objects made and used by Harappans, and its THINK ABOUT IT asks what those objects reveal about what mattered to them.

What mutual accommodation in B.B. Lal's quotation suggests - this concept carries that epigraph, including the line that the Harappan societal scenario was not that of exploitation but of mutual accommodation.

Defining civilisation and explaining at least five key characteristics - the weight of the answer is this concept's seven characteristics, of which the student must give five; the one-line definition comes from the preceding concept.

Describing the town planning of a large Harappan city and what it implies about governance - wide streets, fortifications, upper and lower towns and uniform construction quality are all this concept's content.

Water management illustrated by Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira - this concept holds the hundreds of brick wells at Mohenjo-daro and at least six large reservoirs at Dholavira connected through underground drains, which is exactly the model answer.

Evidence for agriculture and diet and how agriculture supported the cities - this concept has the crops, the plough and the statement that the cities could survive only if enough agricultural produce from rural areas reached them daily.
Common features of the seals and what they suggest about society - steatite, a few centimetres, animal figures with writing signs, and a purpose tied to trade. Already linked and correct.

The Great Bath's significance, the competing readings and why certainty is impossible - this concept sets out all three interpretations, rules out the public bath, and notes we have no inscription, text or traveller's account for it.

Analysing the evidence that the Harappans were relatively peaceful - this concept is where there is no trace of warfare or invasion and no army or weapons of war, an explanation rejected because the evidence it predicts is absent.

Inferring religious or symbolic beliefs from the Priest King, the Dancing Girl and the seals shown in the chapter - this concept is the objects section, where the reader is asked what activities or aspects of life those objects show were important.

How the Indus and Sarasvati river plains contributed to the rise of the civilisation - this concept's geography, fertile plains favourable to agriculture, and towns growing into cities with increasing trade and exchange.

The archaeological evidence for B.B. Lal's mutual accommodation is the uniform quality of construction for small and big houses, which this concept states and explicitly calls the archaeological basis for the chapter's epigraph. The epigraph concept carries the claim but not the evidence.

A settlement with grid-planned streets, baked bricks of uniform size and covered drains identified as Harappan - the leading features are this concept's precise plans, wide streets and uniform construction quality; the seals and drains in the later sub-prompts are secondary to the identification being asked for.

Terracotta figurines from Rakhigarhi - a female figure, a bull and a toy cart - and why such figurines matter when the script cannot be read. This concept is the chapter's objects section, which is exactly about reading a society from the things it left.

A town planner reading Mohenjo-daro's upper and lower towns, its streets oriented to the cardinal directions and the good construction of even smaller houses - every observation in this case is a sentence of this concept.
